steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction and related work section for our benchmarking paper on perturbation-based GNN explainers. It should motivate why GNNs need explanations, go through the main categories of GNN explainers, explain factual vs. counterfactual explanations, and finish with a short contributions subsection.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
GNNs have shown state-of-the-art results in a lot of domains, for example social networks, biological sciences, modeling of physical systems, event detection and traffic modeling. But like other deep learning models, GNNs are black boxes, since they lack transparency and interpretability. This lack of interpretability is a big barrier for using them in critical domains like healthcare, finance and law enforcement. Also, being able to explain predictions is critical for understanding possible flaws in the model and for getting insights to refine it further. So several algorithms have been proposed that explain the inner workings of GNNs to make them interpretable. Fig. 1 shows the diverse landscape of GNN explainability research. We summarize the categories below:

- Model-level: These are also called global explanations. They look at the overall behavior of the model and they search for patterns in the set of predictions that the model makes. Examples are XGNN, GLG-Explainer, Xuanyuan et al. and GCFExplainer.

- Instance-level: These are also called local explainers. They give explanations for specific predictions of a model, for example they reason why a particular instance or input is classified or predicted in a certain way.

- Gradient-based: These follow the idea that the rate of change is represented by gradients. The gradient of the prediction with respect to the input shows how sensitive the prediction is to the input, and this sensitivity gives the importance scores that help to find explanations. Examples are SA and Guided-BP and Grad-CAM.

- Decomposition-based: prediction decomposed and distributed backward layer by layer; scores of input parts = importance; CAM and Excitation-BP, GNN-LRP
- Perturbation-based: perturb input to find important subgraphs (factual or counterfactual); GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, SubgraphX, GEM, TAGExplainer, CF 2, RCExplainer, CF-GNNexplainer, CLEAR, others
- Surrogate: approximate input-output relation locally with interpretable surrogate; GraphLime, Relex, PGM-Explainer

Factual vs. counterfactual:
- factual: minimal subgraph sufficient for same prediction as full graph
- counterfactual: why prediction not made; smallest perturbation changing GNN prediction (edge removal, node feature changes)

## 1.1 Contributions
- systematic study of perturbation-based factual and counterfactual explainers, strengths/limitations
- new insights vs. existing benchmarking literature (App. J)
- seven factual + four counterfactual explainers, first benchmark on counterfactual explainers for GNNs
- deficiencies: stability to noise and variational factors, feasible counterfactual recourses -> open challenges
- public codebase (https://github.com/Armagaan/gnn-x-bench/)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
GNNs have shown state-of-the-art results in a lot of domains, for example social networks, biological sciences, modeling of physical systems, event detection and traffic modeling. But like other deep learning models, GNNs are black boxes, since they lack transparency and interpretability. This lack of interpretability is a big barrier for using them in critical domains like healthcare, finance and law enforcement. Also, being able to explain predictions is critical for understanding possible flaws in the model and for getting insights to refine it further. So several algorithms have been proposed that explain the inner workings of GNNs to make them interpretable. Fig. 1 shows the diverse landscape of GNN explainability research. We summarize the categories below:

- Model-level: These are also called global explanations. They look at the overall behavior of the model and they search for patterns in the set of predictions that the model makes. Examples are XGNN, GLG-Explainer, Xuanyuan et al. and GCFExplainer.

- Instance-level: These are also called local explainers. They give explanations for specific predictions of a model, for example they reason why a particular instance or input is classified or predicted in a certain way.

- Gradient-based: These follow the idea that the rate of change is represented by gradients. The gradient of the prediction with respect to the input shows how sensitive the prediction is to the input, and this sensitivity gives the importance scores that help to find explanations. Examples are SA and Guided-BP and Grad-CAM.

- Decomposition-based: These methods decompose the prediction of the model and distribute it backward layer by layer, and then the score of different parts of the input can be seen as their importance to the prediction. Examples are CAM and Excitation-BP and GNN-LRP.

- Perturbation-based: These use perturbations of the input to find important subgraphs, which serve as factual or counterfactual explanations. Examples are GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, SubgraphX, GEM, TAGExplainer, CF 2, RCExplainer, CF-GNNexplainer, CLEAR, and some others.

- Surrogate: These use the general intuition that in a small range of input values, the relation between input and output can be approximated with interpretable functions. So they fit a simple surrogate model that is interpretable around the prediction. Examples are GraphLime, Relex and PGM-Explainer.

The type of explanation is also an important component. Explanations can be roughly put into two categories, factual reasoning and counterfactual reasoning.

- Factual explanations give insight into the reason behind a specific prediction, by finding the minimal subgraph that is sufficient to give the same prediction as the whole input graph.

- Counterfactual explanations explain why a certain prediction was not made, by giving alternative scenarios that could have led to a different decision. For graphs this means finding the smallest perturbation to the input graph that changes the prediction of the GNN. The perturbations are usually removing edges or modifying node features.

## 1.1 Contributions

In this benchmarking study we study perturbation-based factual and counterfactual explainers in a systematic way, and we find their strengths and limitations with respect to how well they give accurate, meaningful and actionable explanations for GNN predictions. The study brings out new insights that were not studied in the existing benchmarking literature (see App. J for details). Our key contributions are:

- Evaluation that also covers counterfactual explainers: the study covers seven factual explainers and four counterfactual explainers. It is the first benchmarking study on counterfactual explainers for GNNs.

- New insights: our findings show two critical technical deficiencies, stability to noise and variational factors, and generating feasible counterfactual recourses, and these lead naturally to open research challenges.

- Codebase: as a by-product we provide a carefully curated code base that is publicly accessible (https://github.com/Armagaan/gnn-x-bench/).

- Comprehensive evaluation including counterfactual explainers: The benchmarking study covers seven factual explainers and four counterfactual explainers. This is the first benchmarking study on counterfactual explainers for GNNs.

- Novel insights: The findings of our study reveal two critical technical deficiencies, stability to noise and variational factors, and generating feasible counterfactual recourses, which naturally lead us towards open research challenges.

- Codebase: As a by-product, we provide a carefully curated, publicly accessible code base (https://github.com/Armagaan/gnn-x-bench/).
